glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Solomon shows that riches, a large family, and a very long life cannot satisfy when God does not also give the power to enjoy them, then exposes desire that labor never fills and closes with two unanswered questions about what is good for a person and what will happen under the sun after he is gone.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Chapter 6 completes Ecclesiastes 4:1–6:12, Solomon’s look at life in society. It continues straight from 5:18–20, where God gives both wealth and the “power to eat of it,” and its closing questions prepare for the wisdom sayings of chapter 7.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “For who knows what is good for man in life, all the days of his vain life which he passes like a shadow? Who can tell a man what will happen after him under the sun?” (Ecclesiastes 6:12)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Ecclesiastes 6 picks up where chapter 5 left off. Solomon has just called both riches and the ability to enjoy them “the gift of God” (5:19). Now he describes the reverse, an evil he calls “common among men.” God has given a man riches, wealth, and honor, so that he lacks nothing, “yet God does not give him power to eat of it, but a foreigner consumes it” (verse 2). Solomon does not explain why this man suffers, and he does not blame him. He simply shows that having good things and being able to enjoy them are two different gifts.

Then he pushes the case as far as it will go. Imagine a man with a hundred children and “a thousand years twice” of life, whose “soul is not satisfied with goodness” (verses 3, 6). Solomon says “a stillborn child is better than he,” because the child “has more rest than that man” (verses 3, 5). The comparison is meant to shock. It measures how empty a full life can be without satisfaction, and it is not a verdict on the worth of a child or the grief of parents. Both the child and the man end in death: “Do not all go to one place?” (verse 6).

The rest of the chapter widens the point. “All the labor of man is for his mouth, And yet the soul is not satisfied” (verse 7). Solomon commends enjoying what is at hand over “the wandering of desire” (verse 9), yet he keeps even that counsel within the limits of his search. The chapter ends with no human answer to its two questions: what is good for a person, and what will happen under the sun after he is gone (verse 12).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Ecclesiastes 6:1–2 — Wealth Without the Power to Enjoy It

Solomon describes an evil that is common among people: a man receives riches, wealth, and honor from God, yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, and a stranger consumes them instead. The case is the exact reverse of the gift in 5:19, and Solomon calls it “vanity” and “an evil affliction” without explaining why this man suffers.

Ecclesiastes 6:3–6 — A Stillborn Child Compared With an Unsatisfied Long Life

If a man with a hundred children and many years is never satisfied with goodness and does not even receive a burial, Solomon judges that a stillborn child, spared that restless and deprived life, has more rest than he. Even two thousand years without seeing goodness would gain him nothing, and the severe comparison, which weighs earthly experience only, ends where every life ends: “Do not all go to one place?”

Ecclesiastes 6:7–9 — Desire That Labor Never Fills

People work to feed themselves, yet the deeper appetite is never filled, and neither the wise man nor the well-mannered poor man escapes it. Solomon commends “the sight of the eyes,” enjoying what is actually in front of a person, over restless craving, but he adds that this too is “vanity and grasping for the wind.”

Ecclesiastes 6:10–12 — Human Limits and Unanswered Questions

A person’s nature and limits have been set already, and he cannot contend with the One mightier than he, most likely God. Piling up more only adds to what is meaningless, and the chapter closes by asking who knows what is good for man in his brief life and who can tell him what will happen under the sun after he is gone.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Ecclesiastes 6 shows that abundance cannot produce a good life on its own. Wealth, family, and long life are real blessings, but the power to enjoy them is a separate gift from God (5:19; 6:2). Contentment comes from receiving what He gives, not from acquiring more.

The chapter also speaks honestly about loss and dissatisfaction without explaining every case. It gives no reason for the unhappy rich man’s lot, and it does not teach that every unhappy person is under special judgment. Its comparison with the stillborn child should be read with compassion for grieving families.

Finally, the closing questions expose the limits of human knowledge. No one can find by searching what is good in this life or what will happen under the sun after a person is gone. The book’s answer comes through God’s gifts and His final judgment (12:13–14), and the wider witness of Scripture points to Christ, who offers water that ends thirst (John 4:13–14).

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Having without enjoying. Possessions and the power to enjoy them are two separate gifts from God (6:1–2; see 5:19).

Abundance that cannot satisfy. Many children and a very long life cannot make up for a soul that never finds satisfaction (6:3–6).

Desire that labor never fills. Work feeds the body, but the deeper appetite returns (6:7–9; compare 1:8; 5:10).

Contentment with what is at hand. Enjoying what is present is better than restless craving, though even this does not answer the search (6:9).

Human limits before God. No one can contend with the One mightier than himself or know what is good and what lies ahead (6:10–12).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Power to eat of it (6:2). The God-given ability to enjoy what one owns. The phrase echoes 5:19, where God gives this power along with riches.

Stillborn child (6:3–5). A child who dies before birth. Solomon uses the comparison to measure the emptiness of an unsatisfied life, not to judge the child’s worth or to describe the child’s condition after death.

Soul (6:3, 7). Here the inner appetite and longing of a person, which riches and labor never finally fill.

The wandering of desire (6:9). Restless craving that roams after what a person does not have, set against enjoying what is actually in front of him.

Him who is mightier (6:10). Most likely God. A person, as a creature, cannot successfully argue with Him over the lot he has been given.

Vanity (6:2, 4, 9, 11, 12). The NKJV word for a Hebrew term that pictures a breath or vapor, something that cannot be held. In Ecclesiastes it means meaningless: empty and futile when life is pursued without God. In verse 12 it also stresses how brief life is, passing “like a shadow.”

focus: Ecclesiastes 6 completes the book’s reflection on toil and wealth (4:1–6:12) by pressing the contrast drawn in 5:18–20 between owning good things and being given the power to enjoy them: riches, a large family, and an extraordinarily long life all fail to satisfy when that gift is missing. The chapter then turns from these cases to restless human desire and closes with two unanswered questions about what is good and what comes after, exposing the limits of human knowledge just before the wisdom sayings of chapter 7.

sections.title: Wealth Without the Power to Enjoy It
sections.summary: Solomon describes “an evil which I have seen under the sun,” one that is “common among men”: a man has received riches, wealth, and honor from God, yet “God does not give him power to eat of it, but a foreigner consumes it.” This case is the reverse of the gift described in 5:19 and shows that having possessions is not the same as being able to enjoy them.

sections.title: A Stillborn Child Compared With an Unsatisfied Long Life
sections.summary: Solomon pushes the case to an extreme: a man may have a hundred children and many years, yet if his “soul is not satisfied with goodness” and he has no burial, “a stillborn child is better than he,” for the child “has more rest than that man.” Even if he lived “a thousand years twice” without seeing goodness, his life would end where every life ends: “Do not all go to one place?”

sections.title: Desire That Labor Never Fills
sections.summary: “All the labor of man is for his mouth, And yet the soul is not satisfied,” and Solomon asks what advantage the wise man or the poor man who knows how to conduct himself really has. He commends “the sight of the eyes,” enjoying what is actually at hand, over “the wandering of desire,” while the closing words “This also is vanity and grasping for the wind” keep even that counsel within the limits of the search.

sections.title: Human Limits and Unanswered Questions
sections.summary: Whatever a person is “has been named already,” and he “cannot contend with Him who is mightier than he”; adding more only increases vanity, and leaves the question, “How is man the better?” The chapter ends by asking “who knows what is good for man in life” and “Who can tell a man what will happen after him under the sun?”

1.brief: Solomon introduces another painful observation from his examination of life “under the sun,” an evil he has seen for himself and calls “common among men.” The verse only announces the evil and leaves verse 2 to describe it. By calling it common, Solomon signals that what follows is a familiar pattern in human life rather than a rare oddity.
1.explain:
There is an evil which I have seen under the sun continues Solomon’s search within an earthly horizon, life as it appears “under the sun.” He reports an evil he has seen for himself. Chapter 6 follows directly from 5:18–20, where Solomon called the ability to enjoy one’s labor a gift of God.

and it is common among men marks this evil as a familiar pattern in human life, not a rare oddity. The verse only announces the evil; verse 2 describes it.
1.notes: The Hebrew word translated “common” can also mean great or heavy. The NLT reads that it “weighs heavily on humanity,” and the ESV that it “lies heavy on mankind.” Either way, Solomon presents the evil as one that touches many lives.

2.brief: The evil is a man to whom God has given riches, wealth, and honor, so that he lacks nothing he wants, yet “God does not give him power to eat of it, but a foreigner consumes it,” meaning an outsider ends up enjoying what he owned. This case is the exact reverse of the gift described in 5:19, and Solomon calls it meaningless (“vanity”) and “an evil affliction,” attributing both the possessions and the withheld enjoyment to God without explaining why this particular man suffers.
2.explain:
A man to whom God has given riches and wealth and honor begins the case with a man who has everything. Solomon names God as the giver of all of it.

so that he lacks nothing for himself of all he desires adds that every possession he could want is already his.

yet God does not give him power to eat of it, but a foreigner consumes it turns the case. The man cannot enjoy what he has, and an outsider ends up consuming it. This is the exact reverse of 5:19, where God gives a person riches and also the power to enjoy them. Abundance alone cannot produce the good life.

This is vanity, and it is an evil affliction gives Solomon’s verdict: the situation is empty and fleeting, a painful sickness. He attributes both the possessions and the withheld enjoyment to God, but he gives no explanation for why this particular man suffers. The text does not say the man is under special judgment, and it does not offer a diagnosis of his character.

3.brief: Solomon pushes the case to an extreme: a man might have a hundred children and a long life, both counted as rich blessings, yet if “his soul is not satisfied with goodness” and he does not even receive a burial, “a stillborn child is better than he.” The severe comparison measures the emptiness of a life without satisfaction; it is not a verdict on the worth of a child who dies before birth or on the parents who grieve that child.
3.explain:
If a man begets a hundred children and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many pushes the case to an extreme. A hundred children and a long life were among the richest blessings a person could imagine in Israel (Psalm 127:3–5; Proverbs 10:27).

but his soul is not satisfied with goodness, or indeed he has no burial names what is missing. He never enjoys the good he has, and his life ends without even a burial, which in Israel was a mark of disgrace and abandonment (Jeremiah 22:18–19). The text does not explain why he is not buried; it simply adds this to the picture of a life that ends without honor.

I say that a stillborn child is better than he gives a severe verdict. The comparison measures how empty a life without satisfaction is. It is not a judgment on the worth of a child who dies before birth, and it is not a word against grieving parents. Many have known the sorrow of losing a child in pregnancy, and Solomon is not calling such a loss good or preferable. He uses the starkest comparison available to show that even the greatest earthly advantages cannot make up for a life that never knows satisfaction in goodness. Job and Jeremiah used similar language in their anguish (Job 3:11–16; Jeremiah 20:14–18).

4.brief: Solomon describes the stillborn child’s existence as it appears within his earthly horizon: the child “comes in vanity,” “departs in darkness,” and has a name “covered with darkness.” These images picture the obscurity surrounding the child’s arrival, departure, and name in the wider world, not a claim that those who grieve the child never saw, loved, or remembered the child, and Solomon states this loss plainly before explaining in verse 5 why he still judges the child better off than the unsatisfied man.
4.explain:
for it comes in vanity and departs in darkness describes the stillborn child as it appears from Solomon’s earthly vantage point. The child’s coming is a brief breath, and its departure passes unseen by the wider world.

and its name is covered with darkness adds that the child is not known or remembered in public life. These images describe the obscurity of the child’s brief existence in the world. They do not mean that the child was not loved or remembered by those who grieved.

5.brief: Though the child never saw the sun or knew anything, the child “has more rest than that man” whose long, full life never brought satisfaction. Solomon’s point is that the child was spared the restless, unfilled striving of the man’s whole existence; he is weighing earthly experience, not giving a complete account of the child’s condition after death.
5.explain:
Though it has not seen the sun or known anything grants what the child never had: daylight and the experiences of life.

this has more rest than that man gives Solomon’s judgment that the child is better off. The child was spared the restless, unsatisfied striving that filled the man’s long life. Solomon is weighing earthly experience; he is not giving a complete account of the child’s condition after death.

6.brief: Even if the man lived “a thousand years twice,” far beyond any human lifespan, but “has not seen goodness,” the added years would gain him nothing. Solomon’s closing question, “Do not all go to one place?” reminds the reader that the man and the child both end in death and the grave (compare 3:20), so length of life cannot make up for a life without satisfaction.
6.explain:
even if he lives a thousand years twice—but has not seen goodness stretches the man’s life far past Methuselah’s 969 years (Genesis 5:27). The extra years would be worth nothing without enjoyment of what is good, because length of life cannot make up for a life without satisfaction.

Do not all go to one place? closes with a question. The man and the child both end in death and the grave (3:20), so the long unsatisfied life gains nothing over the short one.

7.brief: Solomon turns from particular cases to a general truth: people work to feed themselves, “And yet the soul is not satisfied.” Here “soul” stands for a person’s inner appetite and longing, which no amount of labor finally fills; even after the body is fed, the deeper hunger returns.
7.explain:
All the labor of man is for his mouth turns from particular cases to a general truth: people work to feed themselves.

And yet the soul is not satisfied shows that the hunger remains. Here “soul” stands for a person’s inner appetite and longing. Even after the body is fed, the deeper hunger returns, and human labor never finally fills human desire.
7.notes: The Hebrew word translated “soul” (nephesh) has a wide range of meaning, including life, person, appetite, and throat, which suits a verse that moves from the mouth to the inner longing.

8.brief: Solomon asks two questions that apply this unfilled desire to people who seem better placed than others. Wisdom gives the wise man no exemption from that restless appetite, and the poor man who “knows how to walk before the living,” that is, who conducts himself well among others, gains nothing lasting by it; the questions press the limits of these advantages without denying the real value wisdom has elsewhere (2:13).
8.explain:
For what more has the wise man than the fool? asks what advantage the wise man has. Wisdom gives no exemption from restless, unfilled desire. Elsewhere Solomon affirms that wisdom has real value (2:13); here he presses its limits.

What does the poor man have, Who knows how to walk before the living? asks the same of a poor man who conducts himself well among others. Good conduct is valuable, but it does not fill the deep hunger of the soul.

9.brief: Solomon commends “the sight of the eyes,” enjoying what is actually in front of you, over “the wandering of desire” that roams after what you do not have. Yet he adds, “This also is vanity and grasping for the wind,” keeping even this sound counsel within the limits of the search: contentment is better than restless craving, but contentment alone does not answer the question of lasting meaning.
9.explain:
Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of desire offers counsel. Enjoying what is actually before you is better than desire that roams after what you do not have. Receiving the good that is present is better than chasing what is absent.

This also is vanity and grasping for the wind keeps even this sound counsel within the limits of the search. Contentment is better than restless craving, but it does not answer the question of lasting meaning. This is the last time the phrase “grasping for the wind” appears in the book.

10.brief: Whatever a person is “has been named already”: his nature and limits were set before he arrived, and everyone knows “that he is man,” a creature and not the Creator. For that reason he “cannot contend with Him who is mightier than he,” most likely God, so no one can successfully argue with God over the lot he has been given. The verse acknowledges human limits before God without making human choices meaningless.
10.explain:
Whatever one is, he has been named already says that a person’s nature and limits were set before he arrived. In the ancient world, naming something often meant defining it.

For it is known that he is man states what everyone knows: a human being is a creature, not the Creator. The Hebrew word for man (adam) recalls that humans were formed from the ground (Genesis 2:7).

And he cannot contend with Him who is mightier than he points most likely to God. No one can successfully argue with God over the lot he has been given. The verse acknowledges human limits before God, but it does not make human choices meaningless or turn God’s sovereignty into fatalism.

11.brief: Multiplying the things that increase vanity, whether restless acquisition, striving, or words, only adds to what is meaningless, so Solomon asks, “How is man the better?” The NLT takes the “many things” as words (“The more words you speak, the less they mean”), which links the verse to the futility of arguing with God in verse 10; on either reading, piling up such things or words leaves a person no better off, though the verse does not dismiss the good that God gives to be received and enjoyed (5:19).
11.explain:
Since there are many things that increase vanity observes that many things only add to what is meaningless. These may be restless possessions and striving, or they may be words, especially words used in arguing with God (6:10).

How is man the better? presses the point with a question: piling up such things or words leaves a person no better off. The verse does not dismiss the good gifts God gives to be enjoyed (5:19).
11.notes: The Hebrew word translated “things” can also mean words. The NLT takes it that way: “The more words you speak, the less they mean.” Ecclesiastes 5:2–3, 7 also warns against many words.

12.brief: The chapter ends with two questions that human wisdom cannot answer: “who knows what is good for man in life,” during days that pass “like a shadow,” and “Who can tell a man what will happen after him under the sun?” These remain real questions within Solomon’s search. The question of what is good prepares for the “better” sayings of chapter 7, and the book’s larger answer comes through God’s gifts and His final judgment (12:13–14).
12.explain:
For who knows what is good for man in life, all the days of his vain life which he passes like a shadow? asks what human wisdom cannot fully answer. Life passes like a shadow, brief and fleeting, and no one can say from within it what is truly good.

Who can tell a man what will happen after him under the sun? asks a second question. No one can see the future from within the limits of life under the sun. These remain real questions in Solomon’s search, but they do not mean God can reveal nothing about goodness or the future. The book’s larger answer comes through God’s gifts and His final judgment: “Fear God and keep His commandments, For this is man’s all” (12:13–14).
12.notes: The question of what is good prepares for the “better” sayings that open chapter 7 (7:1–12).
